cards.title: Spread your study out to remember more
cards.body:
Cramming feels productive, but information studied in one long session fades quickly. Spreading the same amount of practice over several shorter sessions, with gaps in between, leads to much better long-term memory. This is called the spacing effect.

Each time you return to the material after a break, you have to work a little to recall it, and that effort strengthens the memory.
cards.apply_it: Split your next study or learning goal into three 20-minute sessions on different days instead of one hour today.

quiz.question: What is the spacing effect?
options: Spreading practice over time improves memory

cards.title: We look for evidence we already agree with
cards.body:
Confirmation bias is our tendency to notice, search for and remember information that supports what we already believe, while overlooking evidence against it. It affects everyone, including experts, and it can make us confident in ideas that are wrong.

The fix is not more intelligence but a habit: deliberately looking for the strongest case against your own view.
cards.apply_it: Pick one belief you hold firmly and spend five minutes finding the best argument against it.

quiz.question: What does confirmation bias make us do?
options: Seek evidence that supports our beliefs

cards.title: How you appraise stress shapes how it feels
cards.body:
Two people can face the same deadline and feel very differently about it. Psychologists describe a two-step appraisal: first we judge whether something is a threat, then whether we have the resources to cope.

When we see a demand as a challenge we can handle, stress tends to energise us. When we see it as a threat beyond our resources, it drains us.
cards.apply_it: For one stressor this week, list three resources you have to handle it: people, skills or time.

quiz.question: In the two-step appraisal, what is the second question?
options: Do I have the resources to cope?
